To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

pulse-height spectra of fission fragments from Cf252 are correlated with the pulse-height response of the surface-barrier detectors used to measure the spectra, that the correlation is due to the fact that the fission fragments are not point sources of ionization but rather have a spatial extent, that the correlation can be used to determine the quality of a given surface-barrier detector used for fission fragment studies, and that the correlation can also be used as an aid in the interpretation of fission-fragment spectra

the pulse-height spectrum parameters of a surface-barrier detector are a function of the detector's bias voltage, resistivity, and thickness and that these parameters can be used to characterize the detector's response to fission fragments.

the pulse-height response of a surface-barrier detector to fission fragments depends on the bias voltage and the resistivity of the detector and that this response can be quantitatively described in terms of a few parameters that are easily determined from a pulse-amplitude spectrum.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new technique for the determination of the energy of fission fragments.
the development of a new technique for the study of fission fragments, the use of surface-barrier solid-state detectors.
the development and testing of solid-state detectors for fission-fragment spectroscopy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the shape parameters associated with a Cf252 pulse-amplitude spectrum may be used to characterize a detector.

the shape parameters of Cf252 fission fragment pulse-amplitude distributions, when plotted against each other, are not random but are related to each other in a way that depends upon detector bias, detector material, detector geometry, and the nature of the detector surface.
pulse-height spectra of fission fragments are not only a measure of detector quality but also a sensitive measure of the quality of the detector biasing system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pulse-height spectra from surface-barrier detectors are not simple and that the spectra are affected by many parameters.
the pulse-height response of a detector for fission fragments is a function of its bias voltage and the detector's resistance.

the pulse-amplitude spectra of surface-barrier silicon detectors are not a simple function of the detector bias voltage and that the shape parameters associated with such spectra are not simple functions of the bias voltage or the detector resistivity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pulse-height response of a detector is a function of the detector's resistivity and bias voltage.
the shape of the fission-fragment spectrum is a function of the bias voltage applied to the detector, the resistivity of the silicon, and the energy loss of the fission fragments in the silicon.
the shape parameter, A2, is a good indicator of detector performance.
